title: Exercise 001
description:
Learn and exercise basic concepts in life and death! Each puzzle contains an easy problem (max level 10k) followed by a solution. Use the solutions to learn Go terms and tricks. Or you can skip them if you already know it.

If you like the puzzles, rate 5 stars so the series can stay visible to other beginners. Happy puzzle solving!

---
source: OGS · Exercises for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: Exercise 001 - solution
description:
To kill a group, you need to prevent your opponent from forming two eyes. An eye is an empty space surrounded by your stones.

Here, a White move at A means that White can form two eyes (marked). The empty space at A1 would be an eye, and the empty space at D1 would be the second eye.

To kill the group, Black has to deny White the move at A that separates the eye spaces and forms two eyes. The only way to do that is to play there first.

Please play at A now and prevent White from making two eyes.
source: OGS · Exercises for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: Exercise 002 - solution
description:
This rectangular six shape is pretty common to see in games. In the corner with no outside liberties, it can be killed. A liberty is an empty point next to a stone or group of stones.

The key move is the placement at A.

B is also conceivable, but it gives White a chance to live. Play on to see why.

title: Exercise 003 - solution
description:
This exercise is about miai. "Miai" is having two different options so that if your opponent takes one, you can take the other. When you have two points in miai, it's not necessary to play there anymore.

Here, C is the only way to live. This makes A and B miai. Play on to see it.

title: Exercise 004 - solution
description:
A typical group needs two eyes to live. If a group is totally surrounded and has only one eye, then the group would be dead.

This group has an eye at A. White can't play at B because the stone would be immediately captured. What is not so certain is whether the space at B-C is really an eye.

The solution is to throw-in at C. This is a tesuji (or tactic) for destroying the eye on the outside.

Please throw in at C.
source: OGS · Exercises for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: Exercise 005
description:
To solve a puzzle, you need to know there are 4 possible outcomes: life, death, ko, and seki. Life means the stones cannot be captured. Death means you can capture all the stones. Ko means there will be alternating captures and the player who can play the last move determines life/death. Seki is mutual life where neither group can kill the other.

What is the status of White's group if Black plays inside next?

A = Alive

D = Dead

K = Ko

S = Seki (both alive)
source: OGS · Exercises for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: Exercise 005 - solution
description:
This shape looks like the twisted four, which is normally alive. But when the group has only one outside liberty (B) Black can make a ko inside.

The answer is A. Any other first move allows White to make two eyes and live.

title: Exercise 012 - solution
description:
This exercise requires knowledge of capturing races. A capturing race is a mutual capturing contest: The first player to put the opponent into atari and capture their stones wins the race.

The diagonal at A is a common first move in these races. It prevents Black from playing at either marked point on the next move. It creates a liberty for White at B while removing a black liberty. So White wins the race by 1 move.

Note: there is also a principle that "eight lives, six dies, and seven depends." Here white has seven stones, so we can assume without reading that white is killable if black plays first.

title: Exercise 014 - solution
description:
There are two ways to tackle a life and death problem of killing a group with a large eye space.

1. Reduce the eye space until it is small enough to be killed. (A)
2. Play directly at the vital point inside the eye space. (B)

Normally, the easier way is to try method 1. But if method 1 does not work, then we have to consider method 2 instead.

title: Exercise 016 - solution
description:
Both A and B kill black. You may recall from Exercise 014 that there are two ways to kill a group with a large eye space.

1. Reduce the eye space until it is small enough to be killed. (A)
2. Play directly at the vital point inside the eye space. (B)

If you applied this lesson, you would have checked A first and conclude that it works. If so, you are on the right track!

B also kills in this case, but there are problems in which B will not kill. In a real-game situation it is more proper to limit eye space before placing a stone inside.

title: Exercise 048 - solution
description:
The only way to kill is to descend with B.

The principle that "the opponent's vital point is my vital point" does not apply in this puzzle. Instead, the solution can be found by the principle of "1-2-3 reading." 1-2-3 reading means finding the obvious move, finding your opponent's response, and then playing that move in advance.

Here, the obvious move is bending at A. White's strongest reply is the throw-in at B. Because the natural move does not work, black should play white's move B in advance.

title: 0: Introduction
description:
This tutorial is meant to help beginners get an idea of stone development. Good stone development will make your local position solid, strong, and efficient, and eventually this good local position will be converted into territory.

The rules of Go are simple, but learning how to build, connect, and develop your stones efficiently is neither easy nor simple. Because Go is complex, it is impossible to memorize all the correct plays in local positions. But by studying standard positions, you can learn what reasonable play looks like and apply it to other cases. That is the purpose of this tutorial.

I assume you are familiar with elementary Go concepts and tactics like atari, liberties, ko, territory, corner, center, tengen, net, and ladder. If you are new to Go, I recommend you look up these terms before starting this tutorial.
hint: Please play at tengen to continue.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 1-1: Liberties
description:
To have good stone development, your stones must have stability (strength) and a direction of development (growth). Let's discuss stability of stones.

Many factors affect the stability of stones: their liberties, their location, their shape, the number of friendly stone nearby, the number of hostile stones nearby, their connectivity to other friendly stones, and the potential for eye shapes. Of these, the most basic factor is the number of liberties.

More liberties typically means a stone is more stable. Think of liberties as a stone's airways. As the liberties are reduced, the stone will suffer a lack of oxygen (metaphorically speaking) and will eventually die.

Here, three stones (ABC) have four liberties, and one stone (D) has three liberties. Stones A to C are more stable than D, which is feeling uneasy because it has fewer liberties.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 1-2: Location of Stones
description: The location of stones is another factor affecting their stability. The main way to fully stabilize stones is to form two eyes, and it's easier to form eyes in a corner than at an edge or the center of the board. See how many moves it takes to form one eye in a corner, on a side, and in the center. Stones near a corner are often the most stable, then stones near the edge of the board, and then stones in the center.
hint: Here, B is the most stable stone because it is located near a corner and has all four liberties. C is weaker than B because C is positioned further from the corner. It will be harder to form eyes than B. The stone at A is third, being farthest from the corner. The stone in the worst position is D because it is short one liberty and surrounds no empty space for eyes.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 1-3: Directions of Development
description:
Think of stones as living things. Each stone has its own life and wants to grow over the whole board. Some stones might be healthy, having many liberties, a comfortable base, plenty of eyes, or many friendly stones nearby. Other stones might be unstable (weak) from a lack of these things.

Let's see what this single stone wants to do here. This stone has four directions to develop (A to D). Why not E? In Go, stones want to develop (grow) along straight lines if possible. Stones aligned in straight lines are more stable than stones aligned in diagonal lines because they can't be separated---each stone shares its liberties with all other stones. In Go terms, straight lines are said to be "thicker" than diagonal lines. I will give more specific explanations and examples in a moment.
hint: Here, the three black stones in the center have a stronger and more powerful position than the three white stones. As a result, Black's position is stronger (thicker) than White's position. By contrast, the three white stones are a bit thin.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 2: Simple Positions of Single Stones
description:
Another consideration in choosing where to play is the stone's potential for development. For maximum development, wide areas are better than narrow ones, the center is better than a side, and a side is better than a corner. Why then are corner plays the standard way of opening? It's because of stability of stones. For stability, a corner is better than a side, and a side is better than the center. (See Puzzle 1-2.) When your stones are stable, you can develop into the sides and the center without worrying about the life of the stones. Stones in the center without connection to a side or corner are like trees without roots. It's hard to settle them and form a stable position.

Here, A is best at making a stable base. But due to its low position it is weak at development to side and center. Moves on the third line from the edge of the board are typically good for making a stable base.

B is closer to the center, so it has better development potential than A. It's also a bit worse for making a base in the corner. Traditionally, stones on the fourth line have more potential for development than stones on the third line, which are good for making a stable base.

C has the best potential for development. (It can move maximally in every direction.) But it's much less stable compared to corner plays because it will need more moves to form eyes.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-1: 4 Basic Moves for Building Local Positions
description: Once you place a stone, the next question is how to develop it. There are four basic tools for developing a good local position: iron pillar (A), one-space jump (B), knight (C.), and diagonal (D). Most moves for getting a favorable local position are made of these basic four development moves, including top-level pro games.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-2: Iron Pillar
description:
A move that makes two or more stones in a row is called an iron pillar. An iron pillar forms a solid and unconditional connection of stones. An iron pillar can never be cut. Solidness is its merit.

The drawbacks of an iron pillar are its slow speed for advancing and lack of flexibility. Sometimes you might want to give up some stones strategically. But for iron pillars, you have only two choices: save all the stones connected by iron pillars or give them all up. There are no other choices for iron pillars.
hint: Please make an iron pillar in the corner.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-3: Iron Pillar - Example of Usage
description: Here is an example of an iron pillar. White played the diagonal, attaching to Black's stone. Against it, Black should make an iron pillar toward the center. Locally, this is the only move. Without more, there is no better move for Black in this local position.
hint: Please answer White's move by forming an iron pillar toward the center. Play at T to see what happens if Black fails to answer White's attachment.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-4: One-Space Jump
description:
A move played one space away from a stone in a straight line is called a one-space jump. This move is used for advancing while keeping a connection between two stones.

Compared to the iron pillar, the one-space jump has its own merit: it advances faster than the iron pillar. You can think about the one-space jump as walking, while the iron pillar is more like crawling.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-5: One-Space Jump - Examples from Pro Game
description:
For a general idea of how to use the one-space jump in a real game, you may observe the following professional game up to move 11. Black was Yamada Kimio 9p (professional 9 dan) and White was Nakano Hironari 9p. The game was played in 2015, although the opening position has been played more times than just these two players.

Right now, getting a general idea of these moves is good enough. It's no problem if you can't see the meaning of each move exactly.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-6: Knight's Move
description:
The next movement option is the knight (also "knight's move" or "knight's jump"), so called because it moves just like the knight in chess.

The knight is a more advanced way to develop a stone compared to a one-space jump or iron pillar. You can think of a knight as an abbreviation of three iron pillars (or a one-space jump and an iron pillar, or an iron pillar and a diagonal). This means that the knight is the "fastest" way to develop stones among the four basic movement options.

Sadly, this merit of the knight comes at some cost: It sacrifices solidness for fast development. It is thin compared to other moves, and sometimes its weak connectivity can bring trouble when your opponent tries to break the connection. Managing the connection weakness is one of the main issues when using the knight.

In the corner marked A, you can see the easiest example of a knight: a corner enclosure. In the opposite corner there's another easy and realistic case of using a knight.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-7: Cutting the Knight
description: This position is the basic form of the knight under the opponent's threat to cut it. A Go proverb says to "strike the knight at the waist." Please cut the two black stones apart by striking at the waist.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-8: Another Knight's Position
description: Here is a more realistic case to show the weak connectivity of the knight and the potential trouble it brings. Please play the following corner pattern.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-9: Diagonal Move
description:
Another basic stone movement is the diagonal. This move is more solid than a one-space jump, but it is also a bit inefficient and dull. It allows inherently less control on the board compared to one-space jump. If that's the case, why, when, and how should you use this move?

First, diagonals are often used to answer a "knight's approach" to get a higher position (Shusaku's diagonal, for Hikaru No Go fans). Second, diagonals are closely related to the knight. They are often used together in local positions because it helps cover the weakness of the knight that you saw before.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 3-10: Basic Use of the Diagonal
description:
In position A, Black and White each have opposing knight's moves. Each player has put down comfortable roots in the corner area, having 4 liberties, and there are no friendly or hostile stones nearby that affect them. Thus, this local position is even and balanced for both presently.

Let's see how to turn this into a more favorable local position for White. One common sequence for this is shown in position B. In this pattern, White plays a knight, which forces Black to crawl along the third line and allows White to develop a nice position.

If Black doesn't want this to happen, how can Black prevent it? The diagonal is an effective tool in this case.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 4-1: Basic Positional Judgement
description:
Correct evaluation of local positions is indispensable for good and reasonable plays in local fights. Many beginner mistakes in local fights stems from their inability to grasp their situation and not from poor reading ability. For example, many beginners ignore a contact play. Generally, a contact play (attachment) creates an "urgent position" because the attachment directly reduces a stone's liberties and threatens stability. But if you don't see the situation correctly, you may see a big advantage in playing elsewhere, and it's easy to repeat this kind of mistake over and over again for a long time without knowing it was a mistake.

In this chapter, I will explain several concepts you should know to evaluate local positions. Starting from simple cases, I will introduce basic principles of positional judgment.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 4-2: More Stones Means More Strength
description:
It is a basic principle that as you invest more stones your stones get stronger and you get a better local position in that area.

In the corner marked A, a black and a white stone are confronting each other. This position is even for both. But in the corner marked B, there are 2 black stones and 1 white stone. The ratio of stones is 2:1. It's easy to see that Black has a better position than White.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 4-3: More Liberties Means More Strength
description:
You already know that liberties are a stone's "means of breathing."

In position A, Black has 8 liberties, but White has 4. Obviously this is a good local position for Black.

In position B, it's even better for Black. Black is hurting the white stone much more severely, as he has 5 and 3 liberties on his groups (we can't say the stones are 100% connected), but White has just 2.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 4-4: More Liberties Means More Strength - more examples
description: Let's consider this more realistic position. Black wants to neutralize the marked white stone and is willing to sacrifice two stones to get that result. The simplest way to do this is shown in the following sequence.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 4-5: Connect Your Stones. Cut Opponent's Stones
description:
Let's consider this position. Black and White each invested 2 stones. Concerning the number of stones, this position is even. In terms of territory, the position is even as well, because neither Black nor White has any secured territory. What about liberties? White's total number of liberties is 6, and Black's 2-stone group has 4 liberties. White has more liberties than Black, although each white stone has fewer liberties compared to Black's group. In terms of liberties, this position is again not bad for White. But if you judge this position according to these criteria, it will mislead you. White has already suffered huge damage.

What makes this position so disastrous for White? It's because of connectivity. The 2 black stones are connected, sharing their liberties with each other. This means whenever 1 stone increases its liberties, the other also gets stronger because the additional "airways" pass from 1 stone to the other through the connection. The 2 white stones do not cooperate in this way. Even if White increases the liberties of 1 stone, this can not affect the liberties on the other stone or provide any instant help to it. As a result, it's twice the work for White to manage the stones than it is for Black. This tough situation for White inevitably will bring a loss of territory. Never allow your stones to be separated like this without huge compensation for this damage.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 5-1: Strength of Stones and Efficiency
description:
In Go, each player tries to maximize the effect of his or her own stones. When a player succeeds in taking bigger advantage of a set number of stones than the other, this difference results in more territory at the end of the game. As I mentioned earlier (somewhat oversimplifying), Go is more about survival of stones than making territory. Moves that build territory but do not threaten the stability of your opponent's stones or stabilize your own weak stones are probably small in value.

Neglecting the strength of each side's stones will decrease the efficiency of the stones and lead to a corresponding loss of territory at the end. This kind of attitude results in small and inefficient play.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 5-2: Simple Case of an Urgent Position
description:
Let's see how this attitude can turn into a loss of territory. In this position, black and white stones touch, removing liberties from each other. Each group has just 4 liberties, no base, and no eye shape. The lack of lack of liberties, lack of base, lack of eye shape, and close distance between stones tells you this is an urgent situation. Both sides are threatening the stability of the other side's stones and are threatened by them at the same time.

For Black, A and B are reasonable moves. A makes White less stable and B makes Black more stable. C and D are worth considering for the same reasons.

The territory-grabbing moves at E and F are "not" reasonable in this case. Although these moves build territory and develop the side area, they ignore the urgency of the position. Each player is currently challenging the stability of the other's stones by removing liberties and beginning to surround the other. A move away from this urgent position will cause Black's stones to become inefficient. You should not play moves with mere territory in mind without considering the "strength of stones." Such moves are small and passive.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 5-3: Real-Game Example
description: Here is a common position where White has invaded Black's corner. White's invasion has left Black with just 4 liberties on the group of 2 stones. Black decides to help the group. Should Black increase the liberties directly with A or should Black secure the side area with B?
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 5-4: Real-Game Example, continued
description:
Let's talk more about why this was an urgent move. When Black played here, White's thinness appeared. White needs to answer it somehow to ensure the stability of the stones.

Please cut through White's position to see what happens if White doesn't block next.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 5-5: 2nd Real-Game Example
description:
Let's try a second example. In this sequence, Black played in the corner first, then White approached on the outside. Black answered with a knight, moving into the side area, and White attached on the side of Black.

Black must now choose how to answer the attachment. Should Black bend under at A or push up with an iron pillar at B? Please consider the shapes you saw in the last two puzzles before choosing your answer.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 6-1: Identifying Bad Moves
description:
The last puzzles highlighted a certain kind of bad move where the move did not increase the player's liberties but only made the opponent's position stronger. This is an instance of a "thank-you move," so called because when you play it, your opponent says "Thank you." :)

I want to teach you to recognize these moves just as easily as you recognize self-atari. Actually, thank-you moves are a related to self-atari.

To grasp the meaning of thank-you moves properly, let us reverse our common goal for a moment and look for bad moves rather than the best ones.
hint: In this hypothetical position, where is White's worst move? It is easy to spot.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 6-2: 2nd Example
description: The last example was easy. Continuing our focus on recognizing bad moves, please find the worst move for White.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 6-3: 3rd Example
description: A subtler case of bad move.
hint: As before, please find the worst move for White.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 6-4: 4th Example
description: This one is a bit harder to recognize. To play a thank-you move, White can move under the Black stone—an effective way to get an unfavorable position by minimizing own liberties.
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)

title: 6-5: 5th Example
description: Here, White played a "diagonal approach" to Black's stone and Black pushed against it. Everything is ok so far. Now, it's White's turn to make a bad move. What can White play to get a really bad local position?
source: OGS · Stone Development for Beginners by mark5000 (CC-BY)
